people.role: Minister of Economy and Planning of Saudi Arabia

briefings.tldr: While the World Bank projects a 400 million youth job shortfall globally, the rapid expansion of AI and digital platforms offers an unprecedented engine for productivity and employment, provided governments, businesses, and educational institutions aggressively coordinate to prioritize entrepreneurship, continuous reskilling, and human-centric industrial policies.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR** 
While the World Bank projects a 400 million youth job shortfall globally, the rapid expansion of AI and digital platforms offers an unprecedented engine for productivity and employment, provided governments, businesses, and educational institutions aggressively coordinate to prioritize entrepreneurship, continuous reskilling, and human-centric industrial policies.

---

## Redefining Skills and the AI Productivity Paradox

* **The AI Value Gap:** According to Peter Brown (Global Workforce Leader at PwC), research from the AI Jobs Barometer indicates that only 20% of organizations are capturing 74% of AI's economic value. These leading companies succeed because they fundamentally redesign work processes rather than simply layering technology over outdated frameworks.
* **The Human Skills Premium:** While technical AI fluency is critical, employers are seeking human-centric skills—such as critical thinking, problem-solving, and qualitative judgment—five times faster for AI-exposed roles. 
  * Candidates possessing these robust human skills command an average wage premium of 25% to 45%.
* **The Entry-Level Experience Paradox:** PwC’s CEO survey revealed a stark market contradiction: 49% of CEOs expect entry-level hiring numbers to decrease, yet 89% of those same CEOs demand that incoming entry-level hires possess higher levels of experience and proven capabilities. 
* **Adapting Traditional Industries:** Chen Jiehui (President of Guangzhou Baiyunshan Pharmaceutical) highlighted how AI is compressing the traditional pharmaceutical "3 10s rule" (10 years, $1 billion cost, 10% success rate for a new drug) to just 5 or 6 years and a fraction of the cost, shifting demand from manual labor to high-level R&D and cellular technology specialists.

## Fostering Entrepreneurship and Decentralized Job Engines

* **Shifting from Job Seeking to Job Creating:** Vijay Eswaran (Executive Chairman of the QI Group) argued that the traditional 9-to-5 corporate career path is failing to keep pace with economic shifts. Educational systems must pivot to cultivate entrepreneurship and prepare youth to build new enterprises rather than compete for dwindling legacy roles.
* **The Myth of the "Solo" AI Founder:** Addressing concerns that AI "agents" will enable solo entrepreneurs to scale without ever hiring employees, Neeti Mehta Shukla (Co-founder and Chief Impact Officer of Automation Anywhere) noted that AI will actually speed up the entrepreneurial lifecycle. While founders may start solo, increased scalability will allow them to hire and expand much faster than previous generations.
* **Democratizing Work Outside Urban Hubs:** To combat the heavy concentration of new jobs in major metropolitan areas, Nourreddine Ouadah (Minister of the Knowledge Economy, Startups and Micro-Enterprises of Algeria) highlighted Algeria's digital freelancer initiative. By creating a simplified online registry, the government enabled 100,000 self-employed youth to secure digital contracts from rural and underserved regions within two years.

## Reforming Policy and Academia through Integrated Collaboration

* **Connecting Industrial and Workforce Strategies:** Peter Brown asserted that economic development, infrastructure investments, and industrial policies should never be designed in isolation. They must feature an integrated workforce strategy that outlines clear, non-negotiable pathways for youth entry, such as mandatory apprenticeship programs.
* **The "Innovate or Pay" Mandate:** In Algeria, the government enacted a policy where legacy corporations must actively co-invest in university-level research, development, and startup incubators. If they choose not to innovate alongside academia, they face an equivalent corporate tax penalty.
* **Transforming University Infrastructure:** Algeria transformed its higher education model by establishing business incubators, early-stage funds, and startup headquarters directly on university campuses. Students are now permitted to submit a functional business plan or a startup launch as their final graduation thesis instead of a traditional academic paper.
* **China's Planned Talent Pipeline:** Chen Jiehui outlined China's highly coordinated model where the government acts as the macroeconomic planner, aligning long-term demographic data with industrial pipelines. In Guangdong province alone, this strategic coordination successfully funneled 1.1 million university graduates into targeted employment sectors last year.

---

## Notable Quotes

> "We are in institutions that were designed in the 18th century with teachers and lecturers from the 19th century preparing students for the 20th and 21st." 
> — **Vijay Eswaran**, Executive Chairman, QI Group

> "If you're still hiring just for domain expertise, you're probably hiring for yesterday." 
> — **Peter Brown**, Global Workforce Leader, PwC

> "Exactly the same thing we were saying about robotics decades ago, today we are saying about artificial intelligence... Now the challenge is in quickly gaining the right skills, because things are moving faster than university curriculums." 
> — **Nourreddine Ouadah**, Minister of the Knowledge Economy, Startups and Micro-Enterprises of Algeria

> "If the workforce is not taken care of... they are your IP, they are your competitive advantage in every form or fashion, doesn't matter which business you are." 
> — **Neeti Mehta Shukla**, Co-founder and Chief Impact Officer, Automation Anywhere

briefings.title: The scientific advances ready to change the world: the Top 10 Emerging Technologies 2026

people.name: Kimmy Bettinger
people.role: Lead, Expert and Knowledge Communities, World Economic Forum

briefings.tldr: The World Economic Forum’s 14th annual Top 10 Emerging Technologies report highlights a paradigm shift toward hyper-personalized healthcare, highly localized production, and AI-driven scientific discovery capable of solving humanity's most pressing infrastructure, environmental, and medical challenges within the next five years.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
The World Economic Forum’s 14th annual Top 10 Emerging Technologies report highlights a paradigm shift toward hyper-personalized healthcare, highly localized production, and AI-driven scientific discovery capable of solving humanity's most pressing infrastructure, environmental, and medical challenges within the next five years.

---

## Reimagining Energy and Climate Adaptation
* **Everything-to-Grid (E2G) Energy:** Converts decentralized nodes—including electric vehicles, rooftop solar, and commercial buildings—into smart, bidirectional assets that can store and feed power back to the grid.
    * *Grid Resilience:* Stabilizes grids during extreme weather-induced demand spikes and balances the massive energy workloads of modern AI data centers.
    * *Hardware Advancements:* Enabled by newer lithium and sodium battery chemistries, rapid-charging hardware, and advanced semiconductor control systems.
* **Direct Lithium Extraction (DLE):** Extracts lithium from brine in hours rather than up to two years, bypassing the need for massive high-altitude evaporation ponds like those in Chile’s Atacama Desert.
    * *Supply Chain Reconfiguration:* Allows extraction and refining to be co-located, potentially smoothing out highly centralized supply chains (currently dominated by China with 62% of refining, Chile with 13%, and Argentina with 11%).
    * *Commodity Pressures:* A steep decline in lithium values (down 80% since 2022) poses an ongoing investment challenge to scaling DLE facilities.
* **Passive Radiative Cooling Materials:** Electricity-free paints, coatings, and window films that cool buildings below ambient temperatures by radiating heat directly into deep space, bypassing the atmosphere.
    * *Energy Savings:* Can cut cooling energy requirements by up to 40%, offering a vital tool for climate adaptation in low-income, high-temperature countries and urban heat islands.
    * *Industrial Utility:* Extends to infrastructure protections, such as specialized power cable coatings that prevent overheating to transmit more electricity.

## Paradigm Shifts in Precision Medicine
* **Personalized mRNA Cancer Vaccines:** Custom-designed therapies created in a matter of weeks by analyzing unique mutations in a patient's tumor biopsy, training their immune system to target specific cancer cells.
    * *Inverting the Blockbuster Model:* Shifts pharmaceuticals away from "one-size-fits-all" chemotherapy toward highly localized, single-patient medical manufacturing.
    * *Cost and Access:* Early-stage custom treatments exceed $100,000 per patient, though hybrid off-the-shelf and personalized vaccine models are being explored to democratize access.
* **Exosome Drug Delivery:** Employs the body’s natural, membrane-wrapped message carriers (exosomes) to deliver therapeutics directly to targeted diseased cells.
    * *Crossing Key Barriers:* Because the body recognizes the courier, exosome-encapsulated treatments can cross the previously impenetrable blood-brain barrier to treat Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s, or target complex cancers.
* **Quantum Simulation for Drug Discovery:** Models molecular interactions directly using quantum physics, bypassing the crude approximations used by conventional computers.
    * *Fixing the Failure Rate:* Aims to lower the current statistic where 9 out of 10 drug candidates fail during clinical trials, altering the economic calculus of drug discovery and making treatments for rare diseases commercially viable.

## Advanced Computing, AI, and Chemical Engineering
* **World Models:** Generative AI systems that learn directly from multi-sensory physical experiences (video, depth sensors, motion) rather than just language and text datasets.
    * *Physical Understanding:* Enables robots to navigate ambiguous factory environments autonomously and builds highly accurate, reactive climate models.
* **Lattice-based Cryptography:** Utilizes multi-dimensional grids and mathematical noise to secure sensitive data in a "fog," future-proofing encryption against upcoming decryption capabilities of quantum computers.
    * *Homomorphic Encryption:* Allows organizations to perform AI analysis on raw data without ever exposing the underlying records, a technique already proven on 300,000 sensitive patient records across multiple hospitals.
* **PFAS (Forever Chemical) Destruction:** Breaks the notoriously resilient carbon-fluorine bond in per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances using specialized electrical currents on electrodes, offering a permanent cleanup solution rather than simple containment.
* **Precision Fermentation:** Programs microbes (like yeast) to synthesize identical proteins, fats, and chemical alternatives traditionally harvested from agriculture or fossil fuels.
    * *Planetary Boundaries:* Offers a scalable food production alternative to feed an estimated 9 billion people by 2050 without additional land, water, or greenhouse gas strain.

## Macro Trends and the New Frontier of Innovation
* **The "Local" and "Personal" Themes:** The 2026 cohort showcases technologies that are shrinking geographic dependencies. This is visible in grid power balanced at the neighborhood level, proteins generated in urban bioreactors, and therapies custom-compounded in local hospital wings.
* **AI Redefining the Scientific Method:** AI is fundamentally shifting scientific discovery away from the standard linear pipeline of "hypothesis, experiment, and validation."
    * *Pre-Hypothesis Experimentation:* Computers now run open-ended, massive data simulations to identify unexpected molecular anomalies first, transforming physical lab work into a final verification step.
* **The Three Obstacles to Tech Scaling:** WEF's 14-year retrospective reveals that breakthroughs typically stall not due to science, but to external bottlenecks:
    * *System Ecosystem Readiness:* Needs complementary systems to catch up (e.g., mRNA was discovered in 2014 but stalled until lipid nanoparticle delivery systems emerged in 2018).
    * *The "First Bet" Risk:* Requires anchor clients, governments, or well-funded companies to adopt crude, highly expensive early iterations.
    * *Regulatory and Policy Frameworks:* Standard-setting bodies must move fast enough to codify security benchmarks, such as standardizing quantum-safe encryption.

---

## Notable Quotes

> "We are starting to hear conversations about the energy demands of AI. When we are already at a point where grids can be really stressed by increasing temperatures and we have this new force coming in, it’s really important that we start to think about how we might reshape that grid." — Kimmy Bettinger

> "Everyone listening to this will know someone who’s been through cancer and cancer treatment, and it always seems like cracking a walnut with a sledgehammer. It’s going to create a lot of damage." — Robin Pomeroy

> "Science traditionally works on: come up with a hypothesis, run an experiment, learn from it, try another experiment. But actually, with AI, what we’re able to do is a bit of experimentation pre-hypothesis... It really shifts the way science is happening." — Kimmy Bettinger

> "While precision fermentation can really offer a new way to meet our needs... we run the risk of pulling that production away from the families and the economies that have been doing that for generations." — Kimmy Bettinger

briefings.title: Top 10 Emerging Technologies 2026

people.name: Mariette DiChristina
people.role: Dean, College of Communication, Boston University

briefings.tldr: The World Economic Forum’s launch of the Top 10 Emerging Technologies of 2026 report highlights breakthrough innovations—including quantum simulation, PFAS destruction, and AI world models—that are redefining scientific possibilities, decoupling resource capabilities from geographic constraints, and demanding agile, non-siloed regulatory frameworks to scale responsibly.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR**  
The World Economic Forum’s launch of the *Top 10 Emerging Technologies of 2026* report highlights breakthrough innovations—including quantum simulation, PFAS destruction, and AI world models—that are redefining scientific possibilities, decoupling resource capabilities from geographic constraints, and demanding agile, non-siloed regulatory frameworks to scale responsibly.

---

## The Track Record of Foresight
The World Economic Forum’s annual report has a proven track record of identifying revolutionary technologies years before they achieve global recognition or major scientific accolades. 
* **Historical Accuracy:** 
  * **CRISPR Gene Editing:** Featured in the 2015 report, five years before winning the Nobel Prize in 2020.
  * **mRNA Vaccines:** Featured in the 2017 report, six years before winning the Nobel Prize in 2023.
  * **AI-Led Molecular Design:** Featured in the 2018 report, two years before DeepMind's AlphaFold breakthrough and six years before winning the Nobel Prize in 2024.

---

## Redefining What is Scientifically Possible
New paradigms in computational power and biotechnology are dramatically lowering the cost of experimentation, allowing scientists to pursue complex, high-stakes hypotheses that were previously considered economically or technically unviable.

* **Quantum Simulation for Drug Discovery:** Traditional drug discovery suffers from a 90% candidate failure rate. Quantum molecular simulation provides unmatched precision over classical computing, identifying and filtering out weak drug candidates early in the pipeline. This makes exploring treatments for rare or complex diseases financially viable.
* **Personalized mRNA Cancer Vaccines:** Enabled by falling genomic sequencing costs and established mRNA manufacturing infrastructure, these therapies use a patient's own tumor biopsy as the exact blueprint to train their immune system to fight specific cancers.
* **AI World Models:** Unlike traditional AI, these data-driven physical AI engines build simulations of physical reality. They can generalize and predict behaviors in complex physical systems even when encountering entirely novel scenarios.
* **Passive Radiative Cooling:** An advanced thermodynamic innovation involving specialized material coatings that reflect solar radiation and emit heat at specific wavelengths, achieving a net cooling effect without consuming electricity.

---

## Decoupling Resource Capability from Geography
Emerging localized technologies are reducing dependence on highly centralized global supply chains and heavy infrastructure, allowing remote or disadvantaged communities to access critical materials, energy, and food.

* **PFAS Molecular Destruction:** Rather than merely containing and relocating toxic "forever chemicals" (PFAS), new chemical technologies are now capable of actively destroying these resilient molecules, offering a permanent solution for polluted soil and water.
* **Everything-to-Grid Energy:** Intelligent optimization platforms allow local communities to link electric vehicles (EVs), building-integrated batteries, and micro-renewables (solar/wind) into self-sustaining local smart grids, bypassing centralized power plants.
* **Direct Lithium Extraction:** Breakthroughs enable localized harvesting of lithium from geothermal and desalination brines, allowing countries without traditional lithium mines to secure battery materials locally.
* **Precision Fermentation:** Utilizing localized biofactories to synthesize specific proteins, vaccines, or food resources. This technology has the potential to dramatically curtail global deforestation and supply chain emissions, though it raises distinct ethical and social transition questions.

---

## Strategic Scaling, Regulation, and the "Future-Back" Approach
As technology advances at an exponential rate, traditional siloed management styles and slow regulatory timelines represent the primary bottlenecks to positive societal impact.

* **The Silo Trap:** Decision-makers frequently evaluate emerging tech through isolated perspectives—such as immediate efficiency, risk mitigation, or regulatory compliance. Successful deployment requires balancing technological, societal, ethical, and regulatory conditions simultaneously.
* **The "Future-Back" Methodology:** Organizations should avoid asking how to implement a technology and instead define the target future state (focused on growth, prosperity, and well-being) and work backward to establish the necessary deployment pathways.
* **Regulatory Agility:** Traditional frameworks cannot keep pace with the speed of technical transformation. Governments must actively utilize regulatory sandboxes and show a willingness to dismantle outdated regulations to foster innovation.

---

## Workforce Evolution and "Critical Doing"
The panel discussed how rapid technological disruption is shifting the demand for human skills, requiring a fundamental redesign of corporate and government training programs.

* **Openness to Change:** With hard technical skills becoming redundant more quickly, the primary skill required of modern workforces is a psychological and structural openness to rapid workflow iteration.
* **Transition to "Critical Doing":** While "critical thinking" remains highly valued, future resilience requires "critical doing"—developing hands-on agility, building collaborative prototypes, and iteratively adjusting tools in real time.
* **AI's True Workplace Value:** Rather than replacing human workforces, advanced AI tools (such as those used in academic publishing) are automating routine administrative tasks, freeing employees to focus on relationship-building, qualitative analysis, and human-level collaboration.

---

## Notable Quotes

> "At least nine out of ten candidates for drug discovery fail... Quantum simulation opens up many, many new disease candidates that all of a sudden become economically worth pursuing."  
> — **Fred Fenter**, *Chief Executive Editor, Frontiers*

> "There are many communities around the world that have polluted water, soil, air... Forever chemicals may now not be forever, and I think that’s a really exciting breakthrough."  
> — **Katherine Daniell**, *Director of the School of Cybernetics, Australian National University*

> "What actually matters is asking an earlier question: what kind of future do we want this technology to enable... and kind of work backwards from that."  
> — **Abdulaziz Al Jaziri**, *Deputy CEO, Dubai Future Foundation*

> "We've done a lot of critical thinking... but the 'critical doing'—how do we actually get our hands on the tools, how do we continue to build together—is one of those skills of the future."  
> — **Katherine Daniell**, *Director of the School of Cybernetics, Australian National University*

briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR** 
Following a highly disruptive regional war in early 2026, the Middle East is navigating a fragile diplomatic off-ramp while rapidly accelerating domestic infrastructure, logistics, and renewable energy projects to build long-term economic resilience.

## Geopolitical Off-Ramps and Ongoing Volatility

* **The US-Israel-Iran Conflict:** A highly disruptive war—triggered by divergent US/Israel objectives and an existential fight for the Iranian regime—disrupted global energy markets and led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz before a ceasefire was reached on April 8th.
* **The Five-Basket Diplomatic Framework:** A signed Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between President Trump and Iranian leadership has initiated a 60-day technical negotiation window targeting five key areas:
    * *Strait of Hormuz:* Reopening, demining, and securing safe maritime passage.
    * *Nuclear Program:* Reaching a final conclusion on long-debated nuclear parameters.
    * *Sanctions Relief:* Delivering economic incentives to Iran from the US, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East.
    * *Guarantees:* Establishing binding frameworks (such as UN Security Council resolutions and regional guarantors) to ensure long-term treaty compliance.
    * *Lebanon and Hezbollah:* Negotiating peripheral parameters to wind down the Israel-Hezbollah conflict.
* **Skepticism and Headwinds:** Hardliners in both Washington and Tehran, coupled with low trust and the upcoming US midterm elections in November, present significant barriers to a final deal, meaning further military friction and inflammatory rhetoric are highly likely during talks.

## GCC Infrastructure Acceleration and Energy Resilience

* **Saudi Arabia's Strategic Pivots:** KSA is shifting investments to prioritize energy resilience, logistics, and alternative transit corridors that bypass the volatile Persian Gulf.
    * *Privatization Momentum:* The National Privatization Center has advanced 160 projects, streamlining public-private partnerships (PPPs) from a typical 12-month cycle to as little as four to six months.
    * *Logistics Hub Expansion:* The Western region is seeing immense traffic, with Jeddah Islamic Port and King Abdullah Economic City processing 15 million containers annually, supported by ports in NEOM, Yanbu, and Jazan.
    * *Alternative Gas Infrastructure:* Aramco's multi-decade Master Gas System projects are accelerating, with Master Gas Phase 4 being moved forward to secure overland energy routes.
* **Renewable Energy and AI Scaling:** Saudi Arabia's renewable energy goals have expanded from 4 GW to 60 GW of current capacity, aiming for 120 GW by 2030. This power is strategically earmarked for AI infrastructure, industrialization, and mobility.
* **Currency Stability and Funding:** Despite the conflict, sovereign currency pegs to the USD have preserved predictable equity returns, keeping international and local banks committed to financing regional infrastructure.

## Shifting Alliances and the Western Influence Vacuum

* **Rising Chinese Influence:** As the US shifts its geopolitical focus, China is aggressively filling the vacuum through technology deployments, green energy investments (solar and carbon capture, utilization, and storage - CCUS), and active diplomatic mediation (e.g., the 2023 Iran-Saudi normalization).
* **The Demise of Western Dominance:** Business leaders note a distinct decline in Western influence across the Arab world, with regional actors increasingly looking to Beijing and self-reliant regional networks.
* **Cooperation vs. Competitive Resilience:** While there is a push to create inclusive regional corridors (incorporating Turkey, Iran, and Israel), there is a competing risk that regional states will build exclusionary, duplicative infrastructure to guarantee unilateral deterrence rather than integrated prosperity.
* **Call for Financial Alternatives:** Corporate leaders highlight the need for a joint Chinese-Saudi reinsurance fund to challenge the London-dominated shipping insurance market, which has driven up global freight costs and inflation due to Strait of Hormuz transit risks.

## The Business Case for Regional Resilience

* **The "Big Brother" Dynamic:** The crisis demonstrated strong intra-GCC coordination, with Saudi Arabia acting as a stabilizer (e.g., hosting diverted civil aircraft from Bahrain and Kuwait during the conflict).
* **Local Company Advantage:** While wars destroy infrastructure (necessitating massive rebuilding bills), local players are increasingly better positioned than global firms to capture reconstruction contracts due to deep-rooted local expertise and a highly educated younger generation.
* **The Scale of the Market:** Despite its global political and energy footprint, the Middle East represents only 3% of global healthcare/pharmaceutical dollar value (compared to 42% for the US and 20% each for Europe and Japan), indicating immense room for market maturity.
* **Generational Shift:** With 60% of the Arab world's population under the age of 18, a new, reform-minded generation is expected to reject historical political frameworks in favor of economic integration and digital-first industries.

## Notable Quotes

> "Geography is destiny. So it’s going to require pragmatic accommodation." 
> — Sanam Vakil

> "The next 10 years for the Middle East will be pivotal in shifting the Middle East from a trade corridor to an industrial and an added value region." 
> — Khalid Sharbatly

> "If you’re crazy enough to live in it, you have to understand it in order to cope, how you can survive on a day-to-day basis." 
> — Mazen Darwazah

> "When you have the government dedicated to go with the private sector for a 20, 25 years program... this government means business. And this means that it is trusted." 
> — Dr. Lena Noureddin

briefings.title: What if Fixing the System Isn’t the Answer?
briefings.tldr: Complex systems cannot be "fixed" like static machines because their challenges are deeply intertwined and constantly evolving; instead, leaders should utilize "workarounds"—creative, low-cost entry points that leverage existing networks, rules, and resources to trigger massive systemic shifts.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR** 
Complex systems cannot be "fixed" like static machines because their challenges are deeply intertwined and constantly evolving; instead, leaders should utilize "workarounds"—creative, low-cost entry points that leverage existing networks, rules, and resources to trigger massive systemic shifts.

***

## The Fallacy of "Fixing" Complex Systems

*   **The Machine Metaphor Failure:** Standard problem-solving assumes systems are like broken machines where a single faulty component can be replaced. In complex systems, this approach fails because problems are deeply intertwined and lack a single root cause.
    *   **Intertwined Systems:** Attempting to solve one issue, such as obesity in healthcare, quickly pulls in food systems, metabolic conditions, and even agricultural fertilizer cycles. 
    *   **Evolving Challenges:** Problems shift as we try to address them. For example, the nature of poverty today is fundamentally different from poverty 100 years ago, and urban poverty looks completely different from rural poverty.
*   **The Power of Entry Points:** If a root cause cannot be isolated, leaders must find accessible "entry points" (often visible symptoms of a problem) to build momentum, learn, and scale change.
*   **Hacker-Inspired Methodology:** Computer hackers excel at finding entry points in systems designed to lock them out. Non-technical leaders can adopt this "hacky" mindset to bypass barriers in education, healthcare, and environmental protection without trying to break down the walls of the system.

## Three Categories of Workarounds

Paulo Savaget identified three distinct patterns of workarounds based on over 100 global case studies:

*   **The Piggyback (Relationships):** This approach involves crossing systems to take a "free ride" on an infrastructure that was never designed for your purpose.
    *   **The ColaLife Example:** In Zambia, life-saving diarrhea medicine was unavailable in remote regions, yet Coca-Cola reached everywhere. The organization ColaLife designed medicine packaging to fit precisely in the unused space between bottles in decentralized Coca-Cola crates.
    *   **Systemic Impact:** This tiny-budget workaround increased medicine uptake from less than 1% to approximately 50% in targeted regions, ultimately prompting policy changes at the World Health Organization (WHO).
*   **The Loophole (Rules):** This approach identifies and exploits legal or procedural gaps for a noble cause.
    *   **Bypassing Academic Paywalls:** Academic research is heavily subsidized by public/philanthropic funds, yet journals charge high fees for access. Savaget and other academics use platforms like *ResearchGate* to upload preprints of their articles. This bypasses paywalls while keeping the work citable.
*   **The Next Best (Resources):** This involves creatively recombining or repurposing discarded or unconventional resources.
    *   **Acoustic Monitoring for Deforestation:** Social entrepreneur Topher White addressed illegal logging in Borneo by repurposing discarded cell phones. Powered by solar energy and placed in tree canopies, the phones "listen" to the forest.
    *   **Real-Time AI Intervention:** An AI program distinguishes the sound of chainsaws from ambient forest noise within a two-kilometer radius and automatically sends a geolocation text alert to local forest patrols.

## Designing, Scaling, and Adapting Workarounds

*   **The Extraordinary and the Mundane:** Successful innovators either find mundane uses for extraordinary technology or extraordinary uses for mundane resources.
    *   **Mundane Use of High-Tech:** Zipline utilized drone technology—initially hyped for commercial retail delivery—for the mundane but life-saving task of transporting blood for transfusions across Rwanda's challenging terrain.
    *   **Extraordinary Use of Low-Tech:** Topher White's use of trash-bin smartphones to halt illegal logging showcases how simple, discarded tools can solve high-level environmental crises.
*   **How Workarounds Scale:** A workaround is not a static silver bullet; it is an entry point. For a workaround to scale, innovators must build momentum, engage with unexpected stakeholders, and adapt. ColaLife succeeded because they redesigned their packaging to serve as a liquid-measuring cup and collaborated with the Zambian Ministry of Health to alter regulations.

## Q&A: Accountability, Hostile Systems, and Cultural Context

*   **The Risk of Relieving Government Accountability:** Somto (Global Shaper, Africa) raised concerns that institutionalizing workarounds might allow failing governments to avoid building permanent public infrastructure. Savaget noted that while this "dark side" exists, many workarounds naturally evolve into the new, highly adaptive default systems of the future.
*   **Cultural Equivalents:** Audience members noted that workarounds are highly prevalent in the Global South, operating under regional terms:
    *   **Jugaad (India):** Resourceful, improvisational innovation born out of severe constraints.
    *   **Jeitinho and Gambiarra (Brazil):** Ingenious ways of bypassing rigid systems using minimal resources.
*   **Navigating Hostile Systems:** Gustavo (Global Shaper, US) asked how to navigate systems that actively close loopholes (e.g., medical debt forgiveness). Savaget explained that closing one loophole usually opens others. He cited Uber's strategy of growing rapidly under unregulated "sharing economy" definitions to become "too big to ban" before regulators could react.

***

## Notable Quotes

> "We are told that we have to fix a system... But this is not how complex systems work... There is no root cause to these problems because not only the problems are intertwined, but the problems change as we try to address them." — Paulo Savaget

> "Hackers taught me that we are wired as humans to look at a system and find an obstacle and think that we have to remove this obstacle. But we constantly find ourselves banging our heads against the wall... [Instead], you don't need to break the walls or the gates to find a way in. You can piggyback." — Paulo Savaget

> "It's not trying to fix a system, it's trying to shift them. It's trying to stir them up. It's trying to adapt, learn, and evolve along with the changes that happen in the system." — Paulo Savaget

briefings.title: When millions of AI agents meet

people.name: Nenad Tomašev
people.role: Senior Staff Research Scientist, Google DeepMind

briefings.tldr: The future of AI is shifting from passive language models to an "agentic economy" of specialized, autonomous systems capable of executing complex, multi-step tasks.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR** 
The future of AI is shifting from passive language models to an "agentic economy" of specialized, autonomous systems capable of executing complex, multi-step tasks. Safely realizing this distributed "society of specialists" requires navigating systemic risks such as human automation bias, web-based agentic traps, and the systemic vulnerabilities of cognitive monoculture.

---

## The Paradigm Shift: From Passive Models to Autonomous Agents

* **Active Execution vs. Text Outputs:** Traditional large language models (LLMs) only generate textual responses to prompts. In contrast, AI agents utilize an LLM "harness" that allows them to observe the state of their environment, make decisions, and execute multi-step actions (such as booking tickets or sending emails) autonomously.
* **The Tools and Technology:** While agentic systems historically operated in narrow, non-linguistic settings (like operational data centers or gameplay), open-source tools like OpenClaw and next-generation platforms like Gemini Spark and Antigravity are rapidly bringing language-capable agents to the mainstream.
* **The Managerial Role for Humans:** Humans are transitioning from active content creators to high-level supervisors and decision-makers who define budgets, set goals, and review agent-proposed plans.
* **The Psychological Risk of Automation Bias:** 
    * **Blind Trust:** As agents successfully complete repetitive tasks, human supervisors naturally begin to over-trust them, switching off active monitoring.
    * **Subtle Failures:** This trust allows highly subtle, non-obvious machine errors or hallucinations to slip through unnoticed, necessitating strict protocols to keep humans actively engaged in the loop.

## The "Society of Specialists" and Agentic Delegation

* **Replicating Humanity-Level Intelligence:** Nenad Tomašev argues that the industry's pursuit of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) should focus on "humanity-level intelligence" rather than "human-level intelligence." Rather than building one massive, expensive, generalist model, the future lies in a distributed network of cheaper, certified specialist models coordinated by a generalist layer.
* **Parallelization vs. True Delegation:** 
    * Current multi-agent workflows primarily rely on basic *parallelization*, where tasks are simply chunked into random sub-parts and run simultaneously.
    * True *intelligent delegation* requires establishing formal contracts between delegator and delegatee agents, complete with protocols for managing delays, verifying subjective preferences, and handling dynamic sub-task failures.
* **Reverse Delegation (AI-to-Human):** In specialized fields like medical radiology, research shows that the most effective teams occur when superhuman, narrow AI models defer and delegate to human experts only when they encounter ambiguous or uncertain data.

## Cybersecurity in an Agentic World: Traps and Monoculture

* **Agentic Traps and Web Poisoning:** Because agents consume the web to execute tasks, malicious actors are building environments designed to exploit them:
    * **Prompt Injection:** Attackers place hidden, non-visual HTML tokens on web pages that redirect the agent's goals without a human supervisor noticing.
    * **Dynamic Cloaking:** Exploitative websites can detect whether a visitor is a human or an agent, serving altered content specifically designed to jailbreak interacting agents.
* **The Risk of Cognitive Monoculture:** 
    * **Correlated Failures:** Because most consumer agents rely on a select handful of dominant foundation models (e.g., Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude), they tend to share identical underlying cognitive biases. 
    * **Systemic Collusion:** When millions of agents make highly correlated decisions, it introduces systemic risks like synchronized financial market "flash crashes" or covert algorithmic auction collusion.
* **Defense through Depth:** Mitigating these risks requires layering multiple defensive strategies, including certifying trusted web sources, strictly limiting agent-granted wallet permissions, and building robust model-level guardrails.

## Transforming Scientific Discovery through Autonomy

* **The Path to Autonomous Research:** The ultimate goal for agentic systems at Google DeepMind is to advance science, medicine, and human welfare by allowing agents to close the loop in automated research laboratories.
* **Physical vs. Digital Safetey:** 
    * In software engineering, agents can easily verify tasks by running automated unit tests.
    * In physical sciences (such as biotech or material battery design), running physical experiments introduces real-world hazards. Agents must operate under strict safety parameters to avoid hardware damage, overheating, or chemical incidents.
* **The Limits of "Combinatorial Closure":** Current agents excel at synthesising, combining, and operating within the boundaries of existing human datasets. However, they have not yet demonstrated the capability to make entirely paradigm-shifting scientific discoveries outside of known human frameworks.

---

## Notable Quotes

> "We see [AGI] not as human-level intelligence... we see it more as humanity-level intelligence where anything that any human may possibly be able to do, but there is no single human that is capable of doing so many things at once."
> — **Nenad Tomašev, Senior Staff Research Scientist at Google DeepMind**

> "Trust is given but it's also earned... Even if it's mostly reliable, it shouldn't be blindly trusted, we should still verify its actions."
> — **Nenad Tomašev, Senior Staff Research Scientist at Google DeepMind**

> "Maybe replicating human-level intelligence isn't the ultimate goal. Maybe the way forward is to replicate humanity-level intelligence instead."
> — **Hannah Fry, Host**
